title: Anomaly detection for epidemiological alert prioritisation
summary: A hybrid unsupervised system that ranks public-health alerts by how unusual they are — catching outbreaks no single method would flag alone.
context: MSc thesis (Machine Learning for Health), built alongside full-time work as a health data scientist

sections.heading: The problem
list: Public health surveillance teams get more open-source alerts than anyone can manually review, most from informal, unverified sources
Collecting alerts was never the hard part — the hard part is figuring out which of the thousands already in the system deserve a person's attention
Most NLP work in this space generates or filters alerts; almost none ranks the ones that already exist

images.alt: System architecture diagram: alerts splitting into Track A and Track B, fusing into a ranked score, then characterisation
images.caption: System architecture — alerts split into Track A and Track B, then fuse into a single ranked score.

sections.heading: Approach
body: End-to-end pipeline: an ETL layer pulls alert text, epi data, geography and timing into one structured data model, feeding a Power BI dashboard and an unsupervised anomaly-ranking layer underneath (no labelled "priority" data exists, so ranking has to be unsupervised). It combines two signals that don't talk to each other:

list: Track A — semantic: embed the alert text, score its distance from the centre of its disease cluster

images.alt: Diagram of Track A: embedding alert text, clustering by disease, and scoring distance from the cluster centre
images.caption: Track A — embed, cluster, then score each alert by its distance from its cluster centre.

list: Track B — structural: an Isolation Forest and an autoencoder over 9 features (severity, geographic spread, recency)
Both scores are percentile-ranked, fused into one hybrid score, and checked against WHO risk criteria with a zero-shot classifier

images.alt: Diagram of Track B: an Isolation Forest and an autoencoder over nine structural features, fused by percentile rank
images.caption: Track B — an Isolation Forest and an autoencoder over nine structural features, fused by percentile rank.

sections.heading: Result
list: The two tracks catch almost completely different alerts — of 2,282 analysed, only 23 scored highly on both

images.alt: Scatter plot showing Track A and Track B scores are nearly uncorrelated across alerts
images.caption: Each dot is an alert. Only 23 of 2,282 scored highly on both tracks — the two signals are almost independent.

list: Fusing them surfaced 68 confirmed outbreaks (yellow fever, Lassa fever, cholera) that never scored extremely high on either method alone — just moderately on both, which no single detector would have caught
Replaced a manual weekly compilation an analyst used to do by hand

images.alt: Correlation heatmap across the semantic score, structural sub-scores, zero-shot score, and the fused hybrid score
images.caption: Spearman correlation across scores — the semantic track (score_A) barely correlates with the structural sub-scores, which is what fusing captures.
